professor_prompt: This week we have been discussing the role of technology in modern education. Some researchers argue that the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence tutoring systems will improve learning outcomes for all students, while others warn it will deepen inequality. In your post, I'd like you to share your perspective on whether AI tutoring systems are ultimately beneficial or harmful for educational equity.

student_a.name: Layla
student_a.post: I think AI tutoring systems are a huge opportunity for students in under-resourced schools. If a student in a rural area gets the same personalized feedback as someone at an elite private school, that's a win for equity. The technology exists — we just need to deploy it fairly.

student_b.name: Marcus
student_b.post: But that assumes equal access to devices and internet, which we don't have. I worry that AI tutoring will just be another advantage for students who are already privileged, while the kids who need help most are left with outdated textbooks and overworked teachers.

professor_prompt: We have been exploring environmental policy this week. A central debate in this field is whether governments should prioritize economic growth or environmental protection when the two appear to conflict. What is your view? Should policymakers be willing to slow economic development to prevent environmental harm, or should economic growth take precedence because it funds future environmental solutions?

student_a.name: Chen
student_a.post: I believe protecting the environment must come first. Once ecosystems are destroyed, no amount of money can restore them. History shows us that short-term economic gains often lead to irreversible long-term damage, like the deforestation of the Amazon.

student_b.name: Priya
student_b.post: Economic growth and environmental protection don't have to be at odds. Wealthier nations can afford cleaner technologies and stricter regulations. If developing countries are forced to prioritize the environment over growth, they may never escape poverty — and poor communities suffer environmental damage the most.

professor_prompt: This week we examined how cities can address housing affordability crises. Two major policy approaches are rent control (limiting how much landlords can charge) and increasing housing supply through deregulation and new construction. Economists disagree on which approach is more effective. What is your view?

student_a.name: Kenji
student_a.post: Rent control keeps long-term residents from being priced out of their neighborhoods. Without it, gentrification displaces entire communities. Whatever the economic theory says, the lived reality for many families is that rent control is the only thing keeping them housed.

student_b.name: Isabelle
student_b.post: But most economists find that rent control reduces the housing supply over time — landlords convert units, reduce maintenance, or sell to owner-occupants. The long-run effect is fewer affordable units. Supply-side solutions like zoning reform are less politically satisfying but more effective.

I used at least one economic or social argument to support my view.
I engaged with Kenji's or Isabelle's specific claim.
My response is at least 100 words.
